unit-m3x.title: Topic 3 · Decimals Extra Practice
unit-m3x.source: Accelerated Math, the teacher's extra-practice sheets on decimals in expanded form and place value

summary.text: Two extra-practice sheets for the decimals unit: writing decimals in expanded form using fractions (like 0.35 = 3 × (1/10) + 5 × (1/100)), writing decimals from their word names, and telling apart a digit's PLACE value (the name of its position) from its DIGIT value (what the digit is actually worth there).

why.text: The unit 1 math test is Thursday 9/10, and expanded form is where a small slip costs the whole answer — one skipped zero or one wrong fraction and the number changes. Practicing with fresh numbers here means you're doing the thinking, not remembering the sheet.

objectives.text: Write any decimal through thousandths in expanded form with fractions, skipping zero digits.
Turn a decimal's word name into numerals, using 'and' as the decimal point.
Name the place value AND the digit value of any digit in a decimal.
Handle the zero cases — a zero inside a number, and a digit whose value is 0.

parentNote.text: Built from the 'extra practice' sheets in the Topic 3 Drive folder — decimals in expanded form (the class writes it with fractions: 2 × (1/10), not exponents), word form to numerals, and place-value vs. digit-value tables. Every number here is fresh, so the sheets stay her homework and this stays extra reps of the same skills. The class's unit 1 test is 9/10 per the newsletter, which is why this ships flagged as test prep. Two spots on the sheet are where kids typically slip and get extra attention here: numbers with an interior zero (like 23.020 — the zero gets skipped in expanded form, and knowing WHICH zeros to skip is the skill), and the underlined-zero row where the digit value is just 0.

nextUp.text: One round, then check the Growth Zone before the 9/10 test.

cards.def:
**Each digit times its place, written as a sum — decimal places as fractions.**
• 0.35 = 3 × (1/10) + 5 × (1/100).
• 47.208 = 4 × 10 + 7 × 1 + 2 × (1/10) + 8 × (1/1000).
cards.hint: Digit × place, plus digit × place, all the way across.

cards.def:
**Tenths (1/10), then hundredths (1/100), then thousandths (1/1000).**
• Each step right is ten times smaller.
• The -ths ending is the giveaway that you're right of the decimal point.
cards.hint: One letter apart, a hundred times different: tens vs. tenths.

cards.term: Skip the zeros in expanded form
cards.def:
**A digit of 0 contributes nothing, so it's left out of the expanded sum.**
• 8.06 = 8 × 1 + 6 × (1/100) — no tenths term at all.
• The zero still matters in the NUMBER (it holds the 6 in the hundredths place); it just doesn't get a term.
cards.hint: Zero holds the seat but doesn't get written in the sum.

cards.term: Word form: 'and' is the decimal point
cards.def:
**The word 'and' marks exactly where the decimal point goes.**
• "Six and four tenths" = 6.4.
• The last word names the final place: "...thousandths" means the number ends in the thousandths place.

**If the words say thousandths, the decimal part needs exactly three digits — pad with zeros to get there.**
• "Five and twelve thousandths" = 5.012, not 5.12.
• Twelve only fills two digits, so a zero slides in front to push it to the thousandths place.
cards.hint: Count the digits the last word demands, then pad.

cards.def:
**Place value is the NAME of the position; digit value is what the digit is WORTH there.**
• In 6.38, the 3's place value is tenths; its digit value is 0.3.
• Two different questions — the table on the sheet asks for both, side by side.
cards.hint: Place = the seat's name. Digit value = the money in the seat.

cards.term: The digit value of a zero
cards.def:
**A zero's digit value is just 0 — whatever seat it sits in.**
• In 67.901, the underlined 0 sits in the hundredths place, and its digit value is 0.
• The place still has a name; the worth is still nothing. Both halves of the answer matter.
cards.hint: Zero anywhere is worth zero — but its seat still has a name.

cards.def:
**To rebuild the number, drop each digit into the place its fraction names.**
• 5 × 1 + 3 × (1/100) → ones digit 5, hundredths digit 3, and a zero holding the empty tenths seat: 5.03.
• Any place with no term gets a zero.
cards.hint: Missing term = zero in that seat.

questions.q: Which is 0.58 written in expanded form?
questions.hint: The first digit after the point is tenths.
steps: The 5 sits in the tenths place: 5 × (1/10).
The 8 sits in the hundredths place: 8 × (1/100).

ex.main: **5 × (1/10) + 8 × (1/100).** Each digit times the fraction for its place.
ex.tip: 5 × 10 + 8 × 1 would be 58 — watch for the whole-number impostor in the options.

questions.q: Which is 0.273 written in expanded form?
questions.hint: Tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths — in order.
steps: 2 is in the tenths place: 2 × (1/10).
7 is in the hundredths place: 7 × (1/100).
3 is in the thousandths place: 3 × (1/1000).

ex.main: **2 × (1/10) + 7 × (1/100) + 3 × (1/1000).** The wrong options shuffle the same digits into the wrong seats — order is everything.
ex.tip: Read left to right and the fractions grow by one zero each step.

questions.q: Which is 7.049 written in expanded form?
questions.hint: What happens to the zero in the tenths place?
steps: 7 is in the ones place: 7 × 1.
The 0 in the tenths place contributes nothing, so it gets NO term.

ex.main: **7 × 1 + 4 × (1/100) + 9 × (1/1000).** Zeros are skipped — writing the 0 × (1/10) term isn't wrong math, but the class convention (and the sheet's examples) leave it out.
ex.tip: The zero still does its job inside 7.049 — it pushes the 4 to hundredths. It just doesn't appear in the sum.

questions.q: A hummingbird egg has a mass of 34.061 grams... okay, a very well-fed hummingbird. Which is 34.061 in expanded form?
questions.hint: Two whole-number places, a zero to skip, then hundredths and thousandths.
steps: 3 × 10 and 4 × 1 cover the whole-number part, 34.
The 0 in the tenths place is skipped.

ex.main: **3 × 10 + 4 × 1 + 6 × (1/100) + 1 × (1/1000).** Same shape as the sheet's robin's-egg problem, fresh number.
ex.tip: Whole-number places multiply by 10s going LEFT; decimal places divide by 10s going RIGHT — the ones place is the hinge.

questions.q: Write "nine and thirty-four hundredths" in numerals.
questions.hint: 'And' is the decimal point; hundredths means two decimal digits.
steps: "Nine" before the 'and' is the whole part: 9.
'And' places the decimal point.
"Thirty-four hundredths" needs exactly two decimal digits: .34 — so 9.34.

ex.main: **9.34.** The last word (hundredths) tells you how many decimal digits there must be.
ex.tip: Say it back to check: 9.34 reads 'nine and thirty-four hundredths.' If your answer reads differently, it's wrong.

questions.q: Write "fifty-one and eight thousandths" in numerals.
questions.hint: Thousandths means THREE decimal digits — how many does 'eight' fill?
steps: "Fifty-one" is the whole part: 51.
"Eight thousandths" needs three decimal digits, but 8 only fills one.
Pad with two zeros in front: .008 — so 51.008.

ex.main: **51.008.** 51.8 says eight TENTHS — a hundred times bigger than eight thousandths. The padding zeros are the whole question.
ex.tip: This is the single most-missed word-form pattern — small number, big place word.

questions.q: Write "four hundred sixteen and two hundred seven thousandths" in numerals.
questions.hint: Everything before 'and' is whole; 'two hundred seven' must fill three digits.
steps: "Four hundred sixteen" is the whole part: 416.
"Two hundred seven thousandths" is 207 filling exactly three decimal digits: .207.
Together: 416.207.

ex.main: **416.207.** The 'and' splits it cleanly — everything after must land in exactly three digits because the last word is thousandths.
ex.tip: 207 already has three digits, so no padding needed this time — but count every time anyway.

questions.q: In the number 45.7, what is the PLACE VALUE of the underlined digit: 45.7̲?
questions.hint: First seat to the right of the decimal point.
steps: The 7 sits one place to the right of the decimal point.
That position is the tenths place.
Place value asks for the position's NAME — not what the digit is worth.

ex.main: **Tenths.** Place value is the seat's name; the digit's worth (0.7) is the next question's job.
ex.tip: 'Sevenths' isn't a place at all — places are named for powers of ten, never for the digit sitting there.

questions.q: Same number, other half of the table: in 45.7, what is the DIGIT VALUE of the 7?
questions.hint: A 7 in the tenths place is worth 7 of what?
steps: The 7 is in the tenths place.
Digit value = the digit × its place: 7 × (1/10).

ex.main: **0.7.** Digit value is what the digit is actually worth in that seat — the place's name (tenths) turned into a number.
ex.tip: The sheet's table asks for BOTH columns on every row: name the seat, then price it.

questions.q: In 82.365, the 6 is underlined: 82.36̲5. What are its place value and digit value?
questions.hint: Count the seats right of the point: tenths, then...
steps: Right of the point: 3 is tenths, 6 is hundredths, 5 is thousandths.
So the 6's place value is hundredths.
Its digit value is 6 × (1/100) = 0.06.

ex.main: **Hundredths, worth 0.06.** Both answers come from the same count — find the seat, then multiply.
ex.tip: The wrong options each get exactly one half right — the sheet's table format punishes half-answers, so practice producing the pair.

questions.q: In 59.408, the 0 is underlined: 59.40̲8. What are its place value and digit value?
opts: Nothing — a zero has no place value
questions.hint: The seat has a name even when the digit is worth nothing.
steps: Right of the point: 4 tenths, 0 hundredths, 8 thousandths — the 0 sits in the hundredths seat.
Its place value is hundredths, exactly like any other digit there.
Its digit value is 0 × (1/100) = 0.

ex.main: **Hundredths, worth 0.** A zero keeps its seat's name but is worth nothing — and it still matters, because it pushes the 8 into the thousandths place.
ex.tip: The sheet has a row exactly like this (67.90̲1) — the zero rows are where the table gets tricky.

questions.q: A number's expanded form is 6 × 10 + 2 × 1 + 5 × (1/1000). What is the number?
questions.hint: Which seats got NO term — and what fills an empty seat?
steps: 6 × 10 + 2 × 1 gives the whole part: 62.
There's no tenths term and no hundredths term — those seats get zeros.
5 × (1/1000) puts a 5 in the thousandths seat: 62.005.

ex.main: **62.005.** Going backwards is the real test of expanded form — every missing term becomes a zero holding its seat.
ex.tip: 62.5 is the trap: it drops the 5 into the first empty seat it finds. Name each seat before placing anything.
